title: Disorder-driven loss of crystalline coherence in two-dimensional electron solids: Quantum Hartree-Fock and classical molecular dynamics
abstract: We investigate the effects of quenched disorder on two-dimensional electron solids using Hartree-Fock theory and classical molecular dynamics. Increasing disorder weakens crystalline correlations, broadens the structure factor, and reduces the measured coherence length toward the pristine lattice spacing. This evolution is consistent with the Imry-Ma and Larkin picture: random pinning disrupts translational order on sufficiently long scales, and stronger disorder reduces the distance over which crystalline organization survives. Classical simulations further show that stronger pinning raises the temperature for particle rearrangement even after crystalline order has disappeared. Disorder thus suppresses structural coherence while stabilizing an amorphous solid against thermal rearrangement.
summary: This work analyzes the effect of quenched disorder on the crystalline order of 2D electron solids using both quantum Hartree-Fock theory and classical molecular dynamics. The research demonstrates that disorder systematically destroys long-range crystalline coherence, leading the system into a stable, amorphous, yet strongly pinned state. This provides a unified picture of structural degradation in disordered quantum matter.
main_problem: The paper investigates how quenched disorder causes the loss of crystalline coherence in two-dimensional electron solids.
main_result: Disorder progressively weakens crystalline correlations, causing a structural crossover from crystalline to amorphous-like states, consistent with the Imry-Ma and Larkin picture.
method: The study employs a combination of continuum Hartree-Fock (HF) theory for quantum treatment and classical molecular dynamics (MD) simulations for classical particle behavior.
model_or_system: The system is a two-dimensional electron solid (Wigner crystal) subjected to quenched random potentials (disorder). The quantum model uses HF theory on an effective Hamiltonian, while the classical model uses MD on Coulomb particles in random wells.
key_observables: Structure factor, coherence length, density contrast, and the ratio of Bragg weight to total density contrast ($f_6$).
important_parameters: Disorder strength (varying Gaussian potential amplitude or impurity concentration), temperature ($T$), and the ratio of disorder strength to electron energy scale ($W/E_F$).
main_assumptions: The comparison is made between two different theoretical frameworks (HF vs. MD) that model disorder differently, and the results are interpreted as a structural crossover rather than a true phase transition.
figures_summary: The figures illustrate the structural crossover from sharp, crystalline peaks in the structure factor to diffuse scattering as disorder increases, and show the evolution of structural diagnostics ($C, f_6$) across different disorder strengths.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the problem by comparing quantum (HF) and classical (MD) approaches. It then details the theoretical framework, showing how disorder weakens correlations, leading to a structural crossover. Finally, it discusses the implications, noting that while pinning can stabilize the amorphous solid, long-range crystalline order is always suppressed.
why_interesting: The interplay between disorder and structural order in 2D electron systems is a cornerstone of condensed matter physics, relevant to understanding amorphous materials and disordered quantum phases.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Single-realization structural crossover diagram using the thresholds stated in the text. The potential uses seed 1701, without averaging. Each colored cell represents one computed parameter value; cell edges are plotting boundaries, not fitted critical lines. Dots identify the sampled parameters. The dashed line is W/EF = rs, corresponding to W = 2H∗/rs, twice the Wigner–Seitz Coulomb scale; it is a reference line, not a fitted boundary. Hartree and HF use identical disorder and discretization.

FIG. 2. Calculated relative density at the indicated rs and disorder amplitudes. Coordinates are physical Cartesian distances in units of the pristine lattice constant aWC; each rhombus is one supercell. The common color scale permits comparison of Hartree and HF. All panels use the same random-potential realization.

FIG. 3. Continuous HF Bragg fractions for the selected states. Points with C < 0.01 are omitted. Lines join sampled values as a visual guide. The horizontal dashed line is the chosen f6 = 0.5 threshold; changing this convention changes the ap- parent structural boundary.

FIG. 4. Classical T = 0 configurations at ne = n0 and increasing impurity density. Blue particles have six Delaunay neighbors, orange fewer, and red more; faint gray points are impurities. Dashed squares show the interior observation region. The lower row is the calculated window-corrected structure factor, Eq. (28), on a common logarithmic color scale. The sharp sixfold peaks broaden and become diffuse as the relaxed structure becomes irregular. All panels use one nested impurity field.

FIG. 5. Positional and bond-orientation correlations at T = 0 and ne = n0. Increasing the impurity concentration broadens the sharp coordination shells and suppresses orientational correlations at larger separation. These are spatial pair averages within one quenched realization; the sampling window and its edge correction are specified in the text.
